content.text: The pendulum is pulled back and then allowed to swing. Which of the following would cause the pendulum to come to rest most quickly?
Replacing the magnet with a stronger one
Shortening the pendulum
Replacing the rod with a heavier one
Connecting the ends of the coil by a piece of copper wire
As the coil swings past the magnet the magnetic flux through it rises and falls, so an emf is induced in the coil. Ask what must be changed for a large current to actually flow.
Any induced current produces its own magnetic field, and that field opposes the motion which created it (Lenz's law). The larger the induced current, the faster the swing is damped.
D

While the pendulum swings, the magnetic flux through the coil changes, inducing a current in the coil. With the coil left as an open circuit no current flows and there is no damping. Connecting the ends of the coil with a copper wire closes the circuit, allowing a large induced (eddy) current to flow; the resulting magnetic force opposes the motion of the coil, by Lenz's law, and the pendulum damps rapidly. A stronger magnet increases the flux change and hence the induced current, so alternatives A and B also increase damping, but closing the circuit enables the current to flow at all and is the critical change; changing the mass of the rod does not significantly change the damping.

Light from a green laser
Microwaves
Radio waves

The two that remain are both electromagnetic, so compare them on the size of the antenna needed to focus them and on the ability of the atmosphere to transmit them.

Light is blocked by cloud and dust and is affected by atmospheric scattering; sound waves cannot propagate through the vacuum of space. Microwaves of a suitable wavelength pass through the atmosphere with little attenuation and can be directed by dish antennas, so they are used for satellite communication. Graph C: current on the vertical axis against speed on the horizontal axis, with a horizontal line at a constant non-zero current.

content.text: While the coil spins it cuts the magnetic field lines, so it induces an emf in itself which opposes the supply voltage. This is called back emf.
The faster the motor turns, the larger the back emf becomes, so the net voltage across the windings falls and the current drawn from the constant-voltage supply falls with it.
A

At zero speed no back emf is induced, so the current is at its maximum and is limited only by the resistance of the windings. As the motor speeds up, the back emf induced in the rotating coil increases and opposes the supply voltage, so the net voltage across the windings, and hence the current, falls. The current therefore decreases asymptotically as speed increases, as shown in graph A.

items: 1 mark: selects the graph consistent with back emf opposing the applied voltage (correct response A, current decreasing with increasing speed).

content.text: Which of the following statements best describes the reason why some materials become superconducting at very low temperatures?
The ions in the superconductor form a regular crystal lattice. There are long channels through the lattice along which the electrons can pass without colliding with the lattice.
Vibrations of the crystal lattice are so small that they do not interfere with the motion of the electrons.
Electrons in a superconductor have very low energy. Their energy is so low that they cannot transfer energy to the crystal lattice in a collision.
Electrons 'pair up'. These electron pairs pass through the crystal lattice of the superconductor without losing energy in collisions with the lattice.
In an ordinary metal the conduction electrons are constantly scattered by the vibrating ions of the lattice, and those collisions are what produce resistance.
Below the critical temperature the electrons no longer behave as independent particles. Think about what they do instead, and about why the lattice can then no longer scatter them.
D

In a superconductor the conduction electrons form Cooper pairs. The paired electrons occupy a collective quantum state and are not scattered by lattice vibrations, so they move through the lattice without transferring energy to it and the resistance falls to exactly zero below the critical temperature.

Which of the following best describes the force propelling the rocket car, and the magnitude of the acceleration of the rocket car while the propellant is being ejected?

content.alt_text: Two-column table headed Force and Acceleration, with four rows of alternatives read in order A to D: (constant, constant), (increasing, constant), (constant, increasing), (increasing, increasing).

| (B) | increasing | constant |
| (C) | constant | increasing |

Force: constant; Acceleration: constant
Force: increasing; Acceleration: constant
Force: constant; Acceleration: increasing
Force: increasing; Acceleration: increasing
Write the thrust as the rate of change of the momentum of the exhaust, $F = \dot{m}v_{exhaust}$, and note exactly what the question says about $\dot{m}$ and about the nozzle velocity.
Then use $a = \frac{F}{m}$ with $m$ the total mass of the rocket car, and follow what happens to that total mass as the propellant is ejected.

The thrust is the rate of change of momentum of the exhaust, $F = \dot{m}v_{exhaust}$. Since the mass flow rate and the nozzle velocity are both constant, the thrust is constant. The total mass of the rocket car decreases steadily as propellant is ejected, so from $a = F/m$ the acceleration of the car increases throughout the burn.

content.text: Name the effect demonstrated by these observations of the lifetimes of the muons.

Both lifetimes belong to the same particle, so the difference cannot be a property of the muon that changed. Ask instead what happens to the rate of a moving clock when it is compared with a stationary one.
Time dilation.

The muons are the same particles in both experiments, so the change in lifetime is not a change in the particle. The lifetime measured in the laboratory, $5.0\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, is longer than the lifetime measured with the muons brought to rest, $2.2\,\mu\mathrm{s}$, so for the laboratory observer the muon is behaving like a clock that runs slow because it is moving. This is time dilation, written $t_v = \frac{t_0}{\sqrt{1 - v^{2}/c^{2}}}$ where $t_0$ is the rest lifetime and $t_v$ is the dilated lifetime measured by an observer who sees the muon moving.

items: 1 mark: names time dilation, the slowing of a moving clock relative to the observer.

content.text: Using either words or calculations, compare the acceleration of the rocket at $t = 20\,\mathrm{s}$ with its acceleration at $t = 100\,\mathrm{s}$.
On a velocity-time graph the acceleration is the gradient, not the value. Compare the slope of the curve at the two times - drawing a short tangent at each point is a reliable way to do it.
The acceleration at $t = 100\,\mathrm{s}$ is greater than the acceleration at $t = 20\,\mathrm{s}$.

Acceleration is the gradient of a velocity-time graph, so it is the steepness of the curve at each instant that matters, not the value of the velocity. The curve is still quite flat at $t = 20\,\mathrm{s}$ and is noticeably steeper by $t = 100\,\mathrm{s}$, so the acceleration at $100\,\mathrm{s}$ is greater than at $20\,\mathrm{s}$. content.text: Account for the shape of the graph over the range of time shown.

Work along the graph in two sections, from lift-off to the peak at about $120\,\mathrm{s}$ and from the peak to the end, and account for each separately because the forces acting are not the same in both.

In the first section the thrust is roughly constant, so use $F_{net} = ma$ and ask what is happening to the mass of the rocket and to the opposing drag. In the second section ask which of those forces has stopped.

From lift-off the engines exert a constant thrust, but the mass of the rocket decreases as fuel is burnt, so $a = F/m$ increases and the gradient steepens. Air resistance also increases with speed, so the rate of increase of velocity diminishes. After about 120 s the fuel is exhausted, thrust ceases, and only gravity acts, giving a constant deceleration.

From lift-off to 120 s the slope of the graph increases: the engine thrust is constant but the mass of the rocket falls as propellant is consumed, so the net force and hence the acceleration increase. The gradient does not stay constant because the opposing drag also increases as the speed changes. After 120 s the engine is no longer burning, the thrust falls to zero, and the only force is gravity, so the velocity decreases at a constant rate, a constant negative gradient, until the graph ends.

content.text: A 30 kg object, A, was fired from a cannon in projectile motion. When the projectile was at its maximum height of 25 m, its speed was 20 m s$^{-1}$. Ignore air resistance.
An identical object, B, was attached to a mechanical arm and moved at a constant speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$ in a vertical half-circle. The length of the arm was 25 m.

content.alt_text: Two side-by-side diagrams. On the left, object A at the top of a parabolic path 25 m above the ground with a horizontal velocity of 20 m per second. On the right, object B at the top of a vertical half-circle 25 m above a pivot, also moving horizontally at 20 m per second, with the ground level marked on both diagrams.

content.text: Both objects are compared at the top of their paths, where each is moving horizontally at the same speed. That the velocity is horizontal at that instant is the crucial fact for both (a) and (c): a horizontal velocity tells you nothing about the vertical motion.

For part (b), treat the fall from the maximum height as a separate journey rather than part of the whole flight. The object begins that part of its motion with zero vertical velocity, so the initial velocity term drops out of the equation you use.

For part (c), work out the vertical acceleration required for each object and compare the resultants, not the individual forces. On one object there is a single vertical force; on the other there are two vertical forces whose resultant must supply the centripetal acceleration of its circular path, which you can calculate from $v^{2}/r$.

2 marks: part (b) sets up the correct relationship and substitutes the given values: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2},\quad u = 0,\quad s = 25\,\mathrm{m},\quad a = …
3 marks: part (c) correctly describes the resultant forces on A and B and correctly deduces that the force on B is greater than the force on A

content.text: Calculate the force acting on object A at its maximum height.

The speed at the maximum height tells you nothing about the forces there, because a horizontal velocity does not make an object accelerate. Ask instead which forces act on the object at that instant and whether they balance.
$294\,\mathrm{N}$

items: 1 mark: calculates the correct force ($F = 294\,\mathrm{N}$, or $30 \times 9.8$).

content.text: Calculate the time it would take object A to reach the ground from its position of maximum height.

Take the fall from the maximum height as a journey of its own rather than as the second half of the whole flight. The object starts that part of its motion with zero vertical velocity, so the time follows from a displacement equation in which the initial velocity term is zero.
The horizontal speed of 20 m s$^{-1}$ is not needed for this part. Check that your answer is of order a couple of seconds, since a fall of about 25 m takes a little over two seconds.
$2.3\,\mathrm{s}$

items: 1 mark: sets up the correct relationship and substitutes the given values: $s = ut + \tfrac{1}{2}at^{2},\quad u = 0,\quad s = 25\,\mathrm{m},\quad a = 9.8\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$
1 mark: correct final answer, $2.3\,\mathrm{s}$, with correct units

content.text: Describe and compare the vertical forces acting on objects A and B at their maximum heights.

Both objects are moving horizontally at their maximum heights, so for B you must first supply whatever vertical acceleration its circular path requires, which is $v^{2}/r$ directed towards the pivot. Compare the resultant vertical forces on the two objects, not the individual forces.

Remember that it is the resultant that produces the acceleration, and that B has two vertical forces where A has only one. For B, decide whether the upward vertical component of the tension is greater or smaller than the weight, and use the required acceleration to decide.

On A the only vertical force is gravity, $mg = 294\,\mathrm{N}$ downwards, so the resultant is $294\,\mathrm{N}$ downwards. On B the vertical forces are gravity downwards and the vertical component of the tension in the arm upwards, and their resultant must provide the centripetal force, so the resultant on B is greater than $mg$ and is directed towards the pivot. The force on B is greater than the force on A.

At the maximum height of both motions the velocity is horizontal, so the vertical acceleration of A is $g$ and the vertical component of the net force on A is $F = ma = mg = 294\,\mathrm{N}$ downwards; gravity is the only vertical force. Object B is travelling in a circle of radius 25 m at 20 m s$^{-1}$, so it has a centripetal acceleration directed downwards towards the pivot of $a = v^{2}/r = 16\,\mathrm{m\,s^{-2}}$, giving a resultant force of $30 \times 16 = 480\,\mathrm{N}$ downwards. On B the downward forces are gravity and the component of the arm's tension; the vertical component of the tension acts upwards and is smaller than $mg$, because the resultant must be the larger centripetal force of 480 N. The force on B is therefore greater than the force on A.

items: 3 marks: correctly describes the resultant forces on A and B and correctly deduces that the force on B is greater than the force on A.
2 marks: correctly describes the resultant forces on both A and B but makes an incorrect comparison, OR correctly describes the resultant force on one of A or B and makes a correct comparison.
1 mark: correctly describes the resultant force on A, OR the resultant force on B, OR makes a correct comparison.

content.text: How does Einstein's Theory of Special Relativity explain the result of the Michelson-Morley experiment?

Start from what was measured, not from the theory: the interference fringes did not shift as the apparatus was rotated, so the round-trip travel time of the light was the same for perpendicular arms at every orientation relative to the Earth's motion, and no aether wind could be detected.

Then connect each postulate to that null result. Ask what each postulate removes (an absolute frame in which light is faster) and then ask what the theory predicts for the length of the arm lying along the direction of motion, which is the effect that cancels out the changed travel time and leaves the round trip invariant.

Special relativity removes the need for an aether: the speed of light is the same in all inertial frames. Michelson-Morley found no detectable difference in the round-trip travel time of light along perpendicular arms for any orientation of the apparatus relative to the Earth's motion. Special relativity explains this by showing that there is no preferred frame, so no apparatus orientation can detect an aether wind, and that along the direction of motion lengths are length-contracted, exactly compensating for the changed travel time and leaving the round-trip time invariant.

Michelson and Morgan found that the interference fringes produced by the two perpendicular light paths did not shift as the apparatus was rotated through 90 degrees, so there was no measurable aether wind and the speed of light appeared the same in all directions. Einstein's first postulate states that the speed of light in vacuum has the same value for all inertial observers, independent of the motion of the source; the second states that the laws of physics are the same in all inertial frames. Together they mean there is no preferred frame of reference, so no experiment of this kind can detect absolute motion through space, and the null result of Michelson-Morley is exactly what special relativity predicts. For an observer in the apparatus frame the length of the arm along the direction of motion is Lorentz length-contracted, which compensates the longer transit time, so the round-trip time is the same for every orientation.

items: 4 marks: demonstrates the link between the Michelson-Morley experiment and the Special Theory of Relativity, an accurate understanding of the results of the Michelson-Morley experiment, AND an understanding of the Special Theory of Relativity.
2-3 marks: demonstrates some understanding of both the Michelson-Morley experiment and the Special Theory of Relativity, OR an accurate understanding of either one of them.
1 mark: references the constant speed of light, OR the absence of an aether.

content.text: The electrical supply network uses a.c. and a variety of transformers between the generating stations and the final consumer. Explain why transformers are used at various points in the network.

Markers look for three areas: what a transformer actually does, what happens to transmission losses when the voltage is changed, and the safety and economic consequences. Make sure you reach all three.

Use $P = VI$ with the power fixed: raising $V$ lowers $I$, and since the loss in the wires is $I^{2}R$ the saving is very large. Also remember a transformer only works on an alternating supply, so the network must be a.c. for these devices to function at all.

Transformers change the a.c. voltage while the frequency is unchanged. Voltage is stepped up at the generating station to reduce $I = P/V$ and hence $I^{2}R$ energy loss in the transmission lines; it is stepped down progressively to safe, useful domestic and industrial voltages. Stepping the voltage down also reduces the danger of electrocution and fire, and reduces the size of the conductors and insulators needed, so transformers improve the safety and environmental cost of the network.

A transformer transfers energy from the primary to the secondary coil by electromagnetic induction and therefore requires an alternating supply to induce an alternating output. Its function is to change the magnitude of the a.c. voltage. In transmission, for a given power $P$, raising the voltage lowers the current, $I = P/V$, and since the resistive loss in the lines is $P_{loss} = I^{2}R$, a high-voltage transmission line wastes far less energy in the cables, which makes it economic to send power over long distances. Near the consumer the voltage is stepped down in stages, because a high voltage is dangerous and would require thick, expensive cables and insulators. The loss in each transformer is small but not zero, so they are made as efficient as possible. Examiners noted that step-down transformers were generally better understood than step-up transformers.

items: 4 marks: clearly and correctly explains why transformers are used, drawing on all three areas: the function of transformers, energy loss in transmission, and safety and environmental issues.
3 marks: clearly and correctly explains why transformers are used referring to two of the three areas above, OR demonstrates a basic knowledge of all three areas.
2 marks: correctly explains why transformers are used referring to one of the three areas, OR demonstrates a basic knowledge of two of the three areas.
1 mark: states one reason.

content.text: A fan that ventilates an underground mine is run by a very large d.c. electric motor. This motor is connected in series with a variable resistor to protect the windings in the coil.
When the motor is starting up, the variable resistor is adjusted to have a large resistance. The resistance is then lowered slowly as the motor increases to its operating speed.
Explain why no resistance is required when the motor is running at high speed, but a substantial resistance is needed when the motor is starting up.
Compare the motor at rest with the motor turning, and in each case ask what is changing the magnetic flux linking the coil and therefore what emf is induced in it.

Use Lenz's law to fix the direction of that induced emf relative to the supply, then note that its magnitude grows with speed, so the current it leaves flowing is progressively smaller. That emf is the quantity the resistance has to work against, not the resistance of the windings themselves.

As the coil of a d.c. motor rotates in the magnetic field, an emf is induced in it that opposes the supply voltage, the back emf. At start-up the coil is stationary, so no back emf is induced and the only opposition to current is the small resistance of the windings; a large current would flow and the windings would overheat. As the motor speeds up the back emf increases, opposing the supply and reducing the current, so once the motor is running at high speed the back emf alone limits the current to a safe value and no external resistance is needed.

The rotating coil cuts magnetic flux and an emf is induced in it. By Lenz's law this induced emf opposes the applied voltage and is therefore called back emf. At start-up the motor is not turning, so the rate of change of flux is zero and there is no back emf; the current is then limited only by the low resistance of the windings, which would give a very large start-up current and could burn them out, so a large series resistance is inserted. As the speed builds, the back emf grows in proportion to the speed and reduces the net voltage across the windings, so the current is progressively reduced. At full speed the back emf is large enough to limit the current to its rated value, and the series resistance can be reduced to zero.

items: 3 marks: a complete explanation involving a description of back emf in motors, the need for protective resistance at low speed, and the production of a back emf at higher speeds that opposes the current through the windings.
2 marks: an explanation that refers to the back emf opposing the current through the windings and states whether the back emf increases or decreases with the speed of the motor.
1 mark: some reference to back emf.

content.text: What is the direction of the force that exists between the two wires?

The stem tells you that both currents run in the same direction. Use the standard result for what happens when the currents in two parallel wires run in the same direction. No numbers are needed here, and do not calculate a force, because only the direction is asked for.
The wires attract each other.

Parallel conductors carrying currents in the same direction attract one another, so the force on wire X is directed towards wire Y and the force on wire Y is directed towards wire X. The result follows from applying the motor effect to each wire in turn: the field produced by wire Y at wire X is perpendicular to the page, and with both currents running to the right the resulting force on each conductor points inwards, towards the other wire. Repulsion is correct only for antiparallel currents, so the 'same direction' in the stem is the discriminating detail and it has to be used. The one mark is for the direction.

items: 1 mark: gives the correct direction, that the wires attract each other.

content.text: In your Physics course you have performed a first-hand investigation to demonstrate the motor effect. Explain how your results demonstrated that effect.

Decide what 'the motor effect' means and write it down before writing anything else: the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, $F = BIl\sin\theta$. The 3 and 4 mark descriptors are only available once your results are tied back to that equation.

List what you actually varied in the investigation - current, the number of turns or the length of wire in the gap, the field strength, the orientation of the coil - and for each one name the factor of the equation it tests. Then say which way the force moved.

The motor effect is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, $F = IlB\sin\theta$. In the investigation a current-carrying wire was suspended between the poles of a magnet, or in a magnetic field, and the force was measured; the force increased when the current was increased, when the length of wire in the field was increased, or when the field strength was increased, and reversed direction when the current or the field was reversed. These trends are exactly those predicted by $F = IlB\sin\theta$, which demonstrates the motor effect.

The rubric here is a four-level explanation rather than a list of facts, so the response has to be an argument: state the effect, describe the investigation, then join each measured trend to one term of $F = BIl\sin\theta$. Describing the apparatus alone, or defining the effect alone, is capped at 1-2 marks; the fourth mark requires the whole chain.

A full response runs like this. The motor effect is the force experienced by a current-carrying conductor placed in a magnetic field, $F = BIl\sin\theta$. A wire was hung between the poles of a magnet and the force was read from a spring balance. The reading increased when the current was increased, so $F \propto I$; it increased when more turns of the same wire were placed in the gap, so $F \propto l$; it increased when the magnets were brought closer together, so $F \propto B$; it was greatest with the plane of the coil parallel to the field, consistent with $\sin\theta = 1$ at $\theta = 90^{\circ}$ and vanishing when the conductor is parallel to the field; and it reversed direction when the battery connections were reversed. Each of those observed trends is exactly what $F = BIl\sin\theta$ predicts, which is what demonstrates the motor effect. Note the trap the examiner report records: attributing the force to an induced back emf, or confusing the motor effect with an electric motor, breaks the link between the measured results and the physics and costs the top marks.

3 marks: the explanation displays a sound knowledge of the physics of the motor effect and relates to the specific investigation undertaken.
2 marks: states the motor effect and describes the investigation but provides no link between the two.
1 mark: either describes the investigation OR states the motor effect.

content.text: Discuss the effects of the development of electrical generators on society and the environment.

Take the two halves of the question in turn. For each, give at least one positive and one negative effect, and for each effect say which physical feature of the generators causes it, since a linked explanation scores far higher than a bare list.

A table with one row per effect is an accepted and well-rewarded format. Avoid writing a long essay that restates the question, and remember that effects on the environment include those arising from how the electricity is generated, not only from the generators themselves.

Positive societal effects include reliable electricity for homes, hospitals, industry and transport, and the development of communications, computing and entertainment. Negative societal effects include the dependence of developed societies on centralised grids, the disruption caused by blackouts, and the electromagnetic and noise pollution near generating and transmission installations. Positive environmental effects include the ability to conserve fossil fuels through efficient electric transport and appliances. Negative environmental effects include atmospheric pollution and greenhouse gas production from the combustion of coal, oil and gas in thermal power stations, the contamination of land and water by mining and by waste from generators, noise pollution, and the heat and warm-water discharge into rivers and oceans affecting aquatic ecosystems.

A response should be structured and address both society and the environment, identifying relevant issues and discussing a positive and a negative aspect of at least one societal effect and at least one environmental effect. Points in point form or in a table are acceptable and are usually well rewarded; unnecessary essay-length responses that restate the question are not.

content.text: Sir William Bragg and his son Sir Lawrence Bragg shared the Nobel prize for physics in 1915 for their work on X-ray diffraction and crystal structure analysis.
Part (a) needs a specific, named example together with a stated purpose. A broad field such as medicine or metallurgy on its own will not earn the marks.

Part (b) is a sequence, and each step is worth marking: the source of the X-rays and its wavelength, what happens to those rays inside the crystal, how the pattern that emerges relates to the arrangement of atoms, and how that pattern is turned into a spacing.

items: 2 marks: part (a) states an example in which an understanding of crystal structure is useful AND states a purpose for this use

content.text: Describe ONE way in which an understanding of crystal structure has impacted on science.
You need two things here: a specific piece of scientific work, and what understanding of crystal structure made possible. Naming a broad area of science on its own is not enough.

Understanding of crystal structure determined the structure of DNA by Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins, whose X-ray diffraction photographs were used by Watson and Crick to build the double helix model. Another example is the use of X-ray diffraction to determine the atomic arrangement of semiconductors such as silicon, which underpins the design of solid-state electronics.

Any one example is acceptable provided the response names the piece of work and states what it made possible. Rosalind Franklin and Maurice Wilkins produced X-ray diffraction photographs of DNA, and the pattern of spots in those photographs is what allowed Watson and Crick to build and then confirm the double-helix model - a direct consequence of understanding that DNA has a regular, crystal-like structure with repeating spacings. An equally acceptable example is the use of X-ray diffraction to determine the atomic arrangement of silicon, which is the basis of designing semiconductor devices and of the whole of solid-state electronics.

items: 2 marks: states an example in which an understanding of crystal structure is useful AND states a purpose for this use.
1 mark: states an example in which an understanding of crystal structure is useful OR a purpose for this use.

content.text: Outline the methods of X-ray diffraction used by the Braggs to determine the structure of crystals.

Set the method out as a chain: a beam of X-rays of known wavelength, a single crystal that is rotated, a record of the directions the X-rays come out in, and then the calculation that turns those angles into a distance.

The key physics is interference between rays scattered from parallel planes of atoms: those rays travel different distances so they add or cancel. Work out the condition for them to add, and be careful about which angle is being used - the one between the ray and the plane, or between the ray and the normal.

The Braggs used a rotating crystal method: a beam of monochromatic X-rays of a known wavelength was directed at a single crystal, which was slowly rotated while the diffracted X-rays were recorded on photographic film or a counter. Rays reflected from parallel planes of atoms inside the crystal travelled different path lengths, so they interfered. Angles of diffraction at which the interference was constructive were measured, and the Bragg relation $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ was used to calculate the perpendicular spacing $d$ between the atomic planes. By varying the orientation of the crystal, the spacings and angles between planes in three dimensions were measured, which allowed the symmetry and the complete atomic arrangement of the unit cell to be deduced.

A full answer should outline that monochromatic X-rays of known wavelength are scattered by the atoms of a single crystal; that the scattered rays from parallel planes travel different distances and interfere constructively at particular angles; that the Bragg condition $n\lambda = 2d\sin\theta$ gives the perpendicular spacing between the planes; and that measuring many such spacings from different orientations allows the three-dimensional atomic arrangement and symmetry of the crystal to be determined.

items: 3-4 marks: provides the general features of the methods used by the Braggs and demonstrates a thorough knowledge of how the crystal structure was determined.
1-2 marks: provides the general features of the methods used by the Braggs and demonstrates only a basic knowledge of how the crystal structure was determined.

content.text: How could the reliability of the experiment be improved?
Reliability is about random error and scatter, so think about what happens to a spread of repeated measurements, and about how many data points the gradient of the best-fit line is being based on.

Repeat each measurement of the threshold frequency and the photoelectron energy several times and calculate a mean, which reduces the effect of random errors. Use a larger number of data points over a wider range of frequencies so that the gradient of the line of best fit is determined more precisely. Use a monochromatic light source of known, stable frequency with a monochromator, and a voltmeter of finer resolution to measure the stopping potential.

Repeating each measurement of the photoelectron energy and of the threshold frequency several times and taking the mean reduces the effect of random errors, so the result no longer depends on one set of readings. Collecting more data points over a wider range of frequencies spreads the gradient of the line of best fit over a longer base, so the scatter of the individual points averages out and the gradient, and hence Planck's constant, the work function and the threshold frequency, are all determined more precisely.

content.text: In the context of semiconductors, explain the concept of electrons and holes.

Build the explanation as a chain: in a pure material the outer electrons are locked in covalent bonds, so there are few carriers; if one is promoted free, a vacancy is left behind; that vacancy can be filled by a neighbouring electron, so it appears to travel; and the direction it appears to travel is what gives it its effective charge.

Be explicit about the carriers in each case — how doping with a Group V and with a Group III impurity changes the relative numbers of electrons and holes, and in which direction each drifts when a field is applied.

In a pure semiconductor the valence electrons are strongly bound to their covalent bonds and there are essentially no free charge carriers, so the material conducts only very poorly. If a valence electron is given enough energy to break its covalent bond it becomes a free, mobile electron in the conduction band, leaving behind a deficiency of one electron in the valence band. This empty site is called a hole. The hole is not a physical particle; it is a convenient description of the state of the valence band, and because an electron from a neighbouring atom can readily move into the vacancy, the hole appears to move through the crystal in the opposite direction to the electrons, as though it were a positively charged particle of charge $+e$. Both the free electrons in the conduction band and the holes in the valence band act as charge carriers, and the conductivity of a semiconductor depends on the number of carriers present. Doping a semiconductor with a pentavalent impurity, such as arsenic in silicon, adds donor electrons that are easily promoted to the conduction band, producing an n-type semiconductor dominated by electrons; doping with a trivalent impurity, such as boron, creates acceptor levels just below the conduction band, so electrons jump from the valence band and leave many holes, producing a p-type semiconductor dominated by holes. Applying an electric field makes the electrons drift one way and the holes the other, so both contribute to the current. Controlling the temperature also controls the carrier concentration, since raising the temperature breaks more covalent bonds and generates more electron-hole pairs.

Start from the bonding picture. In silicon each atom shares its four outer (valence) electrons in covalent bonds with its four neighbours, so at $0\,\mathrm{K}$ the valence band is completely filled and the crystal has essentially no mobile charge; a pure semiconductor therefore conducts only very poorly.

An electron leaves its bond only if it is given at least the band gap energy. A photon can supply that energy directly, and thermal energy breaks bonds as the temperature rises, which is why the conductivity of a semiconductor rises steeply with temperature, the opposite of a metal:

Promoting that electron into the conduction band leaves an unoccupied state in the valence band. The valence electrons of the neighbouring atoms can hop into the vacancy, so what actually travels through the crystal is a succession of electrons while the vacancy appears to travel in the opposite direction. The vacancy is therefore tracked as a particle of charge $+e$, called a hole; it is a convenient description of the state of the valence band rather than a new physical particle.

In an applied field the conduction-band electrons drift towards the positive terminal, against the field, while the holes drift along the field. Both sets of carriers move negative charge in the same direction along the field, so the two currents add and the conductivity is set by how many free carriers are available.

Doping supplies those carriers far more cheaply than thermal excitation. A Group V impurity (P, As, Sb) in silicon contributes one loosely bound extra electron and so gives a donor level just below the conduction band: the material is dominated by electrons and is called n-type. A Group III impurity (B, Al, Ga) contributes one unfilled bond, giving an acceptor level just below the conduction band that captures a valence electron for every impurity atom and leaves a hole behind: the material is dominated by holes and is called p-type.

5-6 marks: demonstrates a knowledge of the major points relating to electrons and holes with amplification of some of them, communicating the ideas effectively.
3-4 marks: demonstrates a basic knowledge of some of the major points relating to electrons and holes, communicating the ideas clearly.

content.text: Read the *shape and the ages* of the two chains before naming anything. One chain is straight with ages increasing steadily along it; the other is curved and much older throughout.
(b)(ii) needs three things: where the magma comes from, why the volcanoes end up in a line, and what the change in trend between the two chains tells you about the plate.
Use the age labels on the map. A chain that gets steadily older in one direction can only be recording motion over time, and that is what identifies the process.

items: (b)(i) Plate tectonics: sea-floor spreading over a stationary hot spot.

(b)(ii) A stationary hot spot in the mantle supplies magma that erupts to form new oceanic crust. The oceanic plate moves steadily over the hot spot, so a new volcano is formed each time the plate passes and the old volcano is carried away with the plate. The volcanoes therefore lie in a straight line, which is the alignment of the chain, and their ages increase steadily with distance from the hot spot, from 0 Ma to 28 Ma for the islands. The seamounts are older submarine volcanoes formed in the same way, with ages from 43 to 63 Ma; the change in the trend of the seamount chain shows that the direction of plate motion changed between the two periods of volcanism, so the two chains record different plate-motion directions.

content.text: (b)(i) One mark: the phenomenon is plate tectonics, demonstrated as sea-floor spreading over a stationary hot spot. Continental drift is also accepted.

(b)(ii) Three marks require the formation *and* the alignment of both chains with some reference to time. The full-credit reasoning is that a linear chain of islands whose age increases steadily away from one end is a hot spot track, written as a plate moves over a fixed mantle plume; the seamounts are the older, submerged volcanoes of the same process, and the different trend of that chain records a different direction of plate motion at the time it was formed.

The examiner report for this question records that most candidates read the island chain as an island arc and ignored the ages on the map. An island arc is curved, is associated with a plate boundary rather than a plume, and shows no linear age progression, so identifying the ages is what separates the top band from the middle one.

content.text: Describe how you carried out a first-hand investigation to determine the relationship between the nature of a surface and the radiation reflected from it.
Markers award marks for four separate things: what you did, what you kept constant, how many times you repeated it, and how the radiation was detected and recorded. Make sure all four appear.

The independent variable is the *nature of the surface*, so change only the surface between trials and record the reflected intensity for each. Keep the angle of incidence, the distance and the source intensity fixed.
Be explicit that the radiation is electromagnetic, that is light from a laser or torch, and place the detector so that it responds only to reflected light and not to the source.

A laser or torch was directed at a small angle onto each of a set of flat surfaces of different nature, such as shiny and dull metal, glass, plastic, paper, cloth, wood and water, viewed through a photometer or detector placed at a fixed angle to the incident beam so that only reflected light reached it. The angle of incidence, the distance and the light source were kept constant, the surface was changed for each trial, and the reflected intensity was recorded. The readings were repeated several times for each surface and averaged, and the results were compared to identify the relationship between the nature of the surface and the amount of radiation reflected.

A strong answer identifies the control of variables, being a constant angle of incidence, constant source intensity and distance, the repetition of trials, and how the reflected radiation was measured and observed. content.text: When the theory of plate tectonics was first proposed, some parts of the scientific community were reluctant to accept it. Discuss the theory of plate tectonics and the evidence leading to its acceptance.
A 'discuss' question worth 6 marks needs all three of: the theory, the evidence for it, and the reasons for the original resistance. Any one of these on its own caps the response well down the band.

For the evidence, the strongest items are the measurable ones: measured sea-floor spreading rates matching the age of the crust, the symmetrical age pattern either side of a mid-ocean ridge, and the actual distribution of shallow- and deep-focus earthquakes and of volcanoes along plate boundaries.

For the resistance, the original objections were methodological rather than observational: no known driving mechanism, a prevailing static-Earth assumption, and the palaeontological evidence being dismissed.

Plate tectonics holds that the lithosphere is broken into rigid plates that move over the asthenosphere, carried by convection currents in the mantle, creating new crust at mid-ocean ridges by sea-floor spreading, destroying it at subduction zones and moving continents. The evidence includes the fit of the continental coastlines and matching fossil and rock formations across ocean basins; the symmetric pattern of oceanic crust either side of mid-ocean ridges with a known age increasing away from the ridge; the measured rates of sea-floor spreading matching the age of the crust; the distribution of shallow-focus earthquakes along mid-ocean ridges and deep-focus earthquakes and volcanoes along subduction zones, corresponding to the plate boundaries; and the polar wander curves and the fit of the continents. The theory was initially resisted in the early twentieth century because it required a mobile Earth when prevailing geological views favoured a static Earth, because continental drift was not supported by a known driving mechanism, and because palaeontologists doubted that landmasses could cross oceans. It was accepted after sea-floor spreading and the palaeomagnetic evidence provided both a mechanism and a direct measurement, and after plate motion was confirmed by accurate sea-floor spreading rates and by the discovery of transform faults.

The response should describe the theory, the evidence, and the reasons for the original reluctance. Examiners reported that most candidates could describe the theory, but few discussed the evidence required by the question.

content.text: Discuss how information gathered from seismic observations has led to greater understanding of the structure of the Earth.
The question is about *inference*, so never describe an observation without also saying what structural conclusion it forces.

Three seismic facts pin down the interior: $S$ waves cannot travel through a liquid, $P$ waves bend as they cross boundaries between layers of different speed, and the difference in arrival time between $P$ and $S$ gives the distance to an earthquake, allowing an epicentre to be triangulated from several stations.

A labelled ray-path diagram showing the concentric layers, the shadow zones and the P and S arrivals is worth a great deal in an 8-mark answer. The examiner report notes that such diagrams were rare and usually unlabelled.

Earthquakes produce seismic waves that travel through the Earth and are recorded at many stations, giving the arrival times of primary, P, and secondary, S, waves. Since P waves travel faster than S waves, the difference in their arrival times at a station gives the distance to the earthquake; with records from many stations the position and depth of the focus can be located, which has led to the recognition of a network of fault lines and a thin, brittle crust beneath the continents. S waves cannot pass through liquids, so their absence beyond the core-mantle boundary, and the S-wave shadow zone, revealed a liquid outer core; refraction of P waves and the behaviour of the core shadow zone showed that the outer core is liquid while the inner core is solid. The speed of P and S waves increases with depth in the mantle, and the variation of wave speed with depth maps zones of differing composition and the solid inner core, while the very low velocities in the asthenosphere mark a partly molten, low-rigidity layer on which the lithospheric plates move. Free oscillations of the whole Earth after a large earthquake give normal modes whose frequencies depend on the density and elasticity of the entire interior, providing an independent check on the layered model.

A strong response links the measured seismic quantities to the structural conclusions: the S-wave shadow zone to a liquid outer core; P-wave refraction and the core shadow zone to a solid inner core; depth-dependent seismic velocities to mantle layering and the asthenosphere; travel-time triangulation to the location of faults; and normal modes to the overall internal structure. A labelled ray-path or layered diagram is very helpful, but examiners noted that such diagrams were rare and usually poorly drawn or unlabelled.

content.text: Optical fibres in medical instruments
(i) asks for the *purpose* of a coherent bundle in an endoscope, so say what the surgeon ends up able to see, and why the word 'coherent' matters.

(ii) is a two-mark description built from two ingredients: which of the core and cladding has the higher refractive index, and the optical process that keeps the light inside the core. A well-labelled ray diagram is an acceptable alternative.

items: (a)(i) A coherent bundle transmits light by total internal reflection so that an image of the interior of the body can be carried out of the body along the fibre, preserving the spatial arrangement of the image points so the surgeon can view the organ being examined.

(a)(ii) The core has a higher refractive index than the cladding, so light entering the core at a sufficiently large angle to the axis strikes the core-cladding boundary above the critical angle and is totally internally reflected, remaining trapped inside the core and travelling along the fibre. The cladding, with a lower refractive index, provides the boundary condition needed for total internal reflection and also protects the core mechanically.

content.text: You have conducted a first-hand investigation to demonstrate the Doppler effect. Describe your investigation and conclusions.
Describe the method, the observations you actually made, and the conclusion. All three are needed for the top band, not just the apparatus.

Decide in advance what quantity your detector is measuring. Connect the microphone to a frequency meter or oscilloscope so that the Doppler shift appears as a change in *frequency*, not as a change in voltage or loudness.

In the conclusion use the words frequency and pitch, and do not describe the effect as a change in loudness. The examiner report for this question records that confusion between loudness, frequency and wavelength was a frequent error.

A source producing a known, constant frequency of sound, such as a signal generator and loudspeaker or a tuning fork, was moved towards a stationary observer, a microphone connected to a voltmeter or frequency meter, and then away from the observer, while the observer remained still; a second trial had the observer moving with the source stationary. The frequency detected was recorded in each case. The results showed that the detected frequency was higher than the emitted frequency when the source approached and lower when it receded, and that the observed shift was greatest for the largest relative speed; with the source stationary the effect was reversed for a moving observer. The pitch, not the loudness, of the sound changed, showing that the Doppler effect is a change of detected frequency, and it demonstrates the relative motion of source and observer.

A strong answer describes the method, the measured results and the conclusion, and distinguishes frequency, pitch, from amplitude, loudness. Examiners reported that a significant error made by many candidates was to say the loudness increased rather than that the pitch increased, indicating confusion between loudness, frequency and wavelength.

items: 3-4 marks: complete description of the investigation methods, results and conclusion.
1-2 marks: partial description of methods and/or conclusion.

content.text: 'CAT scans provide more information than X-rays, so they should be used whenever possible.' Discuss this statement.
The statement contains two claims joined by 'so': that CAT scans provide more information, and that they should therefore always be used. The second claim is the one that needs testing.

Weigh the extra information against the cost in dose of ionising radiation, money and time, and give concrete clinical situations, such as a chest film or a straightforward fracture, where a plain X-ray is the right choice.
Finish with a judgement on the statement. 'Discuss' requires you to commit, and the honest conclusion here is that the premise is right but the conclusion does not follow.

CAT, computed axial tomography, scanning uses a rotating X-ray source and detectors with a computer to reconstruct cross-sectional images, so it gives much more spatial information than a single flat X-ray plate: it can show the position and depth of a structure, separate overlapping organs, and reveal soft tissue detail, and contrast agents and windowing can be used to distinguish tissue types. X-rays remain far cheaper, quicker and involve a much smaller dose of ionising radiation, which is important for children, pregnant women and for repeated imaging; they are also adequate for many fractures and chest films. Therefore, although a CAT scan generally provides more information, it does expose the patient to a higher dose of ionising radiation at greater cost, and so it should be used only when the extra information is needed for diagnosis, not whenever possible. The statement is only partly correct.
A 6-mark discussion is built from four components, taken in this order.

items: Separate the two claims: the premise that a CAT scan gives more information, and the conclusion that it should therefore be used whenever possible.

Information gained by CAT: cross-sectional slices reconstructed by computer, so depth and position are shown, overlapping organs are separated, and soft-tissue detail with contrast agents and windowing distinguishes tissue types, far more than a single flat X-ray plate can give.

Counter-arguments: a plain X-ray is much cheaper, much quicker and involves a far smaller dose of ionising radiation, which matters for children, pregnant women and for repeated imaging, and it remains entirely adequate for many fractures and for chest films.

Judgement: the premise is correct but the conclusion does not follow. A CAT scan should be used when the extra information is needed for diagnosis, not whenever possible, because the radiation dose, cost and time are only justified in that case.
5-6 marks: demonstrates a thorough knowledge of the limitations and advantages of CAT scans as compared with traditional X-rays.
3-4 marks: demonstrates a basic knowledge of the limitations and advantages of CAT scans as compared with traditional X-rays.
1-2 marks: mentions only one or two limitations or advantages of CAT scans or of X-rays.

content.text: Explain why MRI can be used to detect cancerous tissues.

The examiner report for this question is unusually specific: the top band requires the words *magnetic field*, *precession* and *resonance* to be used and explained, and then applied to cancerous tissue. Use all three.

Be clear about what precesses, the hydrogen nuclei in the water of the body, not the electrons and not the field, and make sure the field is described as remaining on throughout, since several candidates wrongly said it was switched off.

The link to cancer is water content: cancerous cells hold more water, so more hydrogen nuclei respond and they relax at different rates. Say explicitly why a plain X-ray cannot distinguish the tissues.

The patient is placed in a very strong, uniform magnetic field, which aligns the nuclei of hydrogen in the body's water molecules with the field. A pulse of radio-frequency electromagnetic radiation is then applied at the Larmor, precession, frequency of the hydrogen nuclei, so the nuclei precess in phase and absorb energy by resonance. When the radio-frequency pulse stops, the nuclei relax and emit the absorbed energy as radio-frequency signals, which are detected by coils and used by a computer to construct an image. The rate of relaxation depends on the density of hydrogen nuclei, so tissues with different water content give different signals, which a simple X-ray cannot distinguish. Cancerous tissue has a greatly increased water content and a different, usually looser, cell structure from normal tissue, so its hydrogen nuclei are not held in the same way and they relax at different rates and give a different signal, which is detected and displayed as a region of different intensity. This is why MRI can identify and delineate cancerous tissue; the field must remain on during the scan, and the precessing hydrogen nuclei, not the field itself, are what is being detected.

A strong answer names and explains the three principles, magnetic fields, precession and resonance, and then applies them to the higher water content of cancerous cells. Examiners reported that very few candidates used the term resonance, many failed to explain precession and what actually precesses, many left out essential steps in the operation of MRI, and a number said that the magnetic field was switched off.

items: 7-8 marks: demonstrates an accurate understanding of the physical principles involved, namely magnetic fields, precession and resonance, AND applies this understanding to explain why cancerous cells can be detected using MRI AND presents the information coherently.
5-6 marks: demonstrates some understanding of the physical principles involved in MRI AND relates this understanding to cancerous cells.
3-4 marks: demonstrates some understanding of some of the physical principles involved in MRI.

1-2 marks: recalls the names of one or two of the physical principles involved, magnetic fields, precession, resonance; OR identifies the water content of cancerous cells as their distinguishing feature.

content.text: Binary stars and their spectra
(i) is a definition, and a definition of binary stars has to say something about how the two stars move relative to each other, not merely that there are two of them.
(ii) asks for the *pattern* in the spectrum, so the word 'periodic' matters as much as the red and blue shifts themselves.

items: (a)(i) Binary stars are two stars that are gravitationally bound to each other and revolve about a common centre of mass, so that they orbit one another with a common period.

(a)(ii) As the two stars orbit their common centre of mass they alternately approach and recede from the Earth. The approaching star shows a blue shift of its spectral lines and the receding star a red shift. The result is a spectrum in which the identified lines shift periodically, first to the red and then to the blue, with a period equal to the orbital period of the system, which identifies the system as a spectroscopic binary.

content.text: (a)(i) The single mark is for a definition that includes the common orbit, not merely a statement that two stars are involved.

(a)(ii) Two marks require the periodic red and blue shift to be described, because the periodicity is what identifies the system as a spectroscopic binary. Merely mentioning that red and blue shifts occur in the spectrum earns 1 mark, which is why many candidates stalled here despite correctly describing the approaching and receding motions.

items: 3 marks: part (a) is worth 3 marks in total, allocated 1 mark(s) to (a)(i) and 2 marks to (a)(ii)

content.text: A student carried out an experiment to examine the spectra of various light sources through spectroscopes as shown in the diagram. The student observed three different spectra. Account for the differences in the three observed spectra.

content.alt_text: Three arrangements of light source, spectroscope and observed spectrum. X: an incandescent lamp viewed directly, giving a full continuous range of colours. Y: a sodium vapour lamp viewed directly, giving two yellow lines on a dark background. Z: an incandescent lamp whose light first passes through sodium vapour and then a spectroscope, giving a range of colours with two black lines.

content.text: Take the three spectra one at a time and identify the *type* of each before you explain it: continuous emission, line emission, or continuous with dark absorption lines.
The explanation for all three is the same physics, the electron energy levels in the source and in the absorber, so once the two sodium levels involved are clear you can write all three.

For the spectrum with dark lines, remember the light reaching the spectroscope is continuous light that has already *passed through* the sodium vapour, so exactly those wavelengths have been removed by atoms being raised between the same two levels that emit in the second case.

Spectrum X is a continuous emission spectrum because an incandescent lamp contains electrons in many energy states that emit photons over a continuous range of energies, corresponding to all visible wavelengths. Spectrum Y is a line emission spectrum because the sodium atoms in the vapour lamp have only a small number of allowed energy levels; the electrons are excited and when they fall back to lower levels they emit only two discrete wavelengths, the two yellow sodium lines, against a dark background, because the hot vapour is not itself a dense incandescent solid. Spectrum Z is a continuous spectrum with two black absorption lines, because the continuous light from the incandescent lamp passed through cool sodium vapour before reaching the spectroscope; the photons in the vapour's two characteristic wavelengths are absorbed by the sodium atoms to raise them between the same two energy levels, so exactly those two wavelengths are missing from the continuous spectrum.

The answer should link each spectrum to the electron energy levels involved: a continuum from electrons in a range of states in the solid filament, discrete emission lines from electrons falling between two discrete levels in the sodium vapour, and two discrete absorption lines because the same transition is driven in the opposite direction by cool sodium atoms. Examiners reported that only some candidates could describe the electron transitions producing emission and absorption spectra, and that some simply restated the stem.

items: 3-4 marks: identifies the differences and provides correct reasons for those differences.
1-2 marks: indicates a basic knowledge and understanding of the reasons for the differences.

content.text: A new generation of Earth-based optical telescopes is advancing optical astronomy. Describe the advances in design that have been incorporated in large telescopes over recent years.
The marks are for advances in *design* and for what each one bought you, being resolution, sensitivity or cost-effectiveness. An advance with no consequence named earns little.

Group them: materials that let much larger mirrors exist at all; active optics that keep a huge mirror within a fraction of a wavelength of shape; adaptive optics that cancel the atmosphere; and segmentation that makes an effective aperture larger than any single mirror.
Stay with Earth-based optical telescopes. Describing space telescopes or radio astronomy is outside the scope of the question, and examiners reported many such responses.

Designs that were impractical for glass have been made possible by the development of very low expansion glasses and, especially, of mirrors made by the polishing and aluminising of ultra-stable materials such as Zerodur and beryllium. Large mirrors are also actively supported and continually realigned by computer-controlled actuators and laser metrology, so that a mirror many metres across can be held to a fraction of the wavelength of the light being observed; this increases resolution, which is limited by the aperture rather than by the mass of the mirror. Adaptive optics uses a wavefront sensor and fast-acting deformable mirrors driven by micro-actuators with response times of a few milliseconds to correct atmospheric turbulence in real time, greatly improving the resolution and sensitivity from the ground and approaching that of a space telescope. Large primary mirrors are segmented, as in the Very Large Telescope and the Gemini telescopes, and the segments are combined interferometrically so that the effective aperture is much larger than any single mirror, increasing both resolution and light-gathering power. Adaptive optics and active optics make the cost of achieving a given collecting area and resolution far lower, since the required mirror diameter need not increase in proportion. Narrow-band filters, laser guide stars and charge-coupled devices further improve the sensitivity and usable dynamic range. Many of these advances are cheaper, more reliable and more adaptable than placing large optical telescopes in orbit, which is why the new generation remains Earth-based.

A strong answer names the advances, being new materials such as Zerodur, beryllium and carbon-fibre mirrors, active optics with laser metrology, segmented primaries, adaptive optics with deformable mirrors and laser guide stars, and improved detectors and filters, and links each to an improvement in resolution, sensitivity or cost-effectiveness. Examiners reported that many candidates described developments outside the scope of the question, and that only some could describe correctly how these advances result in improved telescope performance.

3-4 marks: demonstrates a basic knowledge of recent advances in telescope design and gives some indication of how these developments led to improvements in resolution, sensitivity, or cost-effectiveness.
1-2 marks: mentions only one or two recent advances in telescope design.

content.text: Explain how the data presented in Hertzsprung-Russell diagrams may be used to understand the evolution of stars.
Explain what the two axes of the diagram represent and name the groups stars fall into before you describe any evolution.
The marks are won by linking each stage of a star's life to a *movement* on the diagram, and by saying what determines the direction of that movement, which is the star's mass.

Draw the diagram with the evolutionary track on it. Examiners reported that most candidates left out the sketch, and that a common error is to place the protostar at the top right; it starts at the bottom right and moves up and left onto the main sequence.

A Hertzsprung-Russell diagram plots luminosity, or absolute magnitude, against surface temperature, and stars fall into distinct groups: the main sequence, giant and supergiant stars, and white dwarfs. A star of a given mass begins as a protostar in the lower right of the diagram, contracts and heats up, and joins the main sequence at a position set by its mass; more massive stars lie higher and to the left and are hotter, larger and more luminous. When core hydrogen fusion is exhausted a star of about the mass of the Sun leaves the main sequence, expands to become a red giant, up and to the right, fusion proceeds in shells, and the core contracts to a white dwarf, down and to the left, with the envelope lost as a planetary nebula. A star of more than about three solar masses leaves the main sequence to become a red supergiant, fuses heavier elements up to iron, and then ends as a neutron star or black hole. Because mass determines the position on the main sequence and the time a star spends there, the distribution of the plotted points, and the number of stars in each evolutionary phase, gives information about the ages and evolution of star populations, such as the globular and open clusters. Thus the H-R diagram converts measured luminosities and temperatures into a picture of the life cycle of stars.

A strong answer relates each evolutionary stage to a group on the H-R diagram and describes the characteristics of each group, and normally includes a sketch of the H-R diagram with the evolutionary track marked. Examiners reported that most candidates did not draw a H-R diagram and could only provide a poor description of it, and that many mistakenly believed a protostar is located at the right-hand top corner of the diagram or that stars move up and down the main sequence.

content.text: The nucleon

content.text: Describe how you carried out a first-hand investigation to determine the penetrating power of alpha, beta and gamma radiation on a range of materials.
Markers award marks for four things: what you did, what you kept constant, how you detected and recorded the radiation, and how many times you repeated it.
The independent variable is the absorber, so change the material and the thickness and change nothing else, including the distance from source to detector and the exposure time.

Examiners reported that many responses read as though a computer simulation had been used, so describe apparatus you could physically set up in the laboratory and name the absorber for each type of radiation.

A radioactive source of each type of radiation was used with a suitable detector, or a film badge or diffusion chamber, at a fixed distance behind a range of absorber sheets of different materials and thicknesses, such as aluminium foil, paper, plastic and lead. The source, its distance from the detector and the time of exposure were kept constant; only the absorber was changed, acting as the control. The detected count rate, or the degree of blackening of the film, was recorded for each absorber. Alpha radiation was stopped by a few centimetres of air or a sheet of paper, beta radiation by a few millimetres of aluminium, and gamma radiation required several centimetres of lead, so the relative penetration of the three types was established. Each measurement was repeated several times and averaged, and the count rate with no absorber was used as a control to confirm that the source output was constant.

A strong answer explicitly discusses the control of variables, the repetition of trials and how the radiation was measured and observed, and explains how the range of absorber materials and thicknesses was used to compare penetration. Examiners reported that many candidates gave the impression they had used a computer simulation and did not discuss reliability or the use of a control.

3 marks: correctly describes an appropriate experiment including any two of the specific points.
2 marks: correctly describes an appropriate experiment including one of the specific point.
1 mark: provides a partial description of an appropriate experiment.

content.text: The Manhattan Project is the codename given to the development of atomic (nuclear fission) bombs during World War II. Discuss the significance of this project for society.
This is a 'discuss' question: you must weigh positive against negative consequences for society, and a one-sided answer caps your mark.

The positive case is the peaceful one, namely nuclear power, isotopes in medicine and industry, and the demonstration of fission itself. The negative case is Hiroshima and Nagasaki, the arms race, and the culture of secrecy the project fostered.
Finish with an overall judgement about the legacy, and be prepared to say something about the responsibility of the scientists involved.

The project brought together a large international scientific effort that produced the first nuclear chain reaction and the first atomic bomb, demonstrating the enormous energy released by nuclear fission and leading directly to the development of nuclear power stations and to the use of radioactive isotopes in medicine, industry and research; it also established large-scale national science policy, funding and international scientific cooperation during and after the war. Its negative effects were devastating: the destruction of Hiroshima and Nagasaki killed many thousands of civilians, showed that a single weapon could destroy a city, and began the nuclear arms race, in which the superpowers built ever larger arsenals, tested bombs in the atmosphere, and held the world close to nuclear annihilation through the Cold War. The secrecy and the culture of secrecy it fostered damaged trust between scientists and governments, as later revealed in cases such as the withholding of information about radiation hazards. Its legacy for society is therefore both the peaceful applications of nuclear science and the permanent threat posed by nuclear weapons, together with the ethical debates about the responsibility of scientists for the consequences of their work.

The response should weigh positive and negative effects on society. Examiners reported a wide variation in performance, with the most successful candidates conversant with the history of the period and giving a discussion appropriate to the scope of the question; most provided responses that were insufficiently detailed.

items: 5-6 marks: demonstrates a thorough knowledge of the positive and negative effects of the Manhattan Project on society.
3-4 marks: demonstrates a sound knowledge of the positive and negative effects of the Manhattan Project on society.
1-2 marks: mentions only one or two effects of the Manhattan Project on society.

content.text: Analyse how Chadwick's and Fermi's work resulted in a greater understanding of the atom.

Treat the two scientists separately first, giving apparatus, observation and inference for each, and only then combine them. Examiners reported that many candidates answered as though the two had worked together.

For Chadwick the decisive point is that the radiation could not be deflected in electric or magnetic fields and yet had a mass comparable with the proton, so it could not be gamma radiation, and that conservation of energy and momentum in collisions with nuclei of known mass fixed the particle mass.

For Fermi the decisive points are the slow-down of neutrons by wax, their capture by nuclei, and the production of new radioactive isotopes from uranium. Note also that the identification of barium as a fission product was his interpretation of the work of others, and that many candidates wrongly credited him with discovering the neutrino.

Chadwick investigated the radiation emitted by beryllium when bombarded with alpha particles, which had been found by the Joliot-Curies but which they wrongly believed to be gamma rays. Chadwick showed that this radiation was uncharged, penetrated matter only weakly compared with gamma rays but could not be deflected in electric or magnetic fields, and had a mass close to that of the proton. Using conservation of energy and of momentum for the collisions of the particles with nuclei of known masses such as nitrogen, he showed that the particles must have a mass about the same size as a proton, so they could not be photons. He therefore identified a new neutral particle, the neutron, adding it to the proton as a constituent of the nucleus and completing the picture of the nucleon composition of the nucleus, since neutrons explain why the measured atomic masses exceed the sum of the proton masses. Fermi's work, by contrast, concerned the neutron itself. He showed that neutrons slowed by passing through paraffin wax were much more likely to be captured by a nucleus, which allowed nuclear reactions to be studied systematically, and he used neutron bombardment of uranium to produce new radioactive isotopes, showing that neutrons can be absorbed by nuclei and showing the transmutation of elements. Together with the work of Hahn, Strassmann and Meitner, whose identification of barium as a fission product he correctly interpreted, Fermi's results revealed nuclear fission and led to the first controlled chain reaction. The two scientists therefore advanced the understanding of the atom in complementary ways: Chadwick completed the nuclear model by identifying its neutral constituent, and Fermi revealed the reactions through which nuclei can be transformed and the energy that they release.

A strong answer describes the apparatus, the observations and the inference for each scientist separately, and then analyses their combined contribution. Many candidates believed that Fermi discovered the neutrino and nuclear fission, and a significant number answered as if Chadwick and Fermi worked together, so the two sets of work should be kept clearly distinct.

items: 7-8 marks: the answer demonstrates an extensive knowledge of the work of both scientists, expressed coherently, and shows an analysis of how their work contributed to an understanding of the atom.
5-6 marks: the answer includes a thorough description of the work of both scientists, and how their work led to an understanding of the atom.
3-4 marks: the answer shows a basic knowledge of the work of both scientists; OR demonstrates a sound knowledge of the work of one scientist.
1-2 marks: the answer shows a limited knowledge of the work of both scientists; OR shows a basic knowledge of the work of one scientist.

content.text: Transducers and light meters
State the name of the transducer that is commonly used in a light meter of a camera.
The device must have no power supply of its own and must change its electrical property purely because of the light falling on it.
For the relationship, decide whether a graph of resistance against light intensity is a straight line through the origin, and what happens to the curve at high light levels.
A light-dependent resistor (LDR), also called a photoresistor. (a)

A light meter has to measure light without a power supply, so it needs a passive two-terminal device. An LDR is a semiconductor whose conductivity increases as photons free electrons from covalent bonds, so more light means more charge carriers and hence less resistance.

content.text: Transducers and light meters
Describe the relationship between the amount of light incident on the transducer referred to in part (a)(i), and its resistance.

The resistance decreases as the incident light intensity increases, but not in simple proportion: it falls steeply at low light levels and then levels off towards a small constant resistance at high light levels.

The relationship is inverse but non-linear: resistance falls monotonically as intensity increases while the rate of decrease drops off, so the resistance-intensity graph is a decreasing curve that flattens. The reason is that at high light levels nearly all the available charge carriers have already been freed, so further increases in intensity add very few extra carriers.

content.text: An ideal differential-input operational amplifier is connected into the following circuit.

content.alt_text: Circuit of an op-amp: an input of Vin = +0.4 V goes through a 25 kilohm resistor to the inverting, minus, input; a 500 kilohm feedback resistor connects the output back to the inverting input; the non-inverting, plus, input is connected to ground; the output is taken across a pair of terminals labelled Vout.

content.text: Explain the function of the 500 k$\Omega$ resistor in this circuit.
Follow the feedback path: the 500 k$\Omega$ resistor connects the output back to one of the inputs. Ask what would happen to the circuit without it.
With negative feedback the two inputs of an ideal op-amp sit at the same potential. Work out that potential from the grounded input, then use the fact that no current enters the op-amp.
Once you have the current through the 25 k$\Omega$ resistor, the output must be whatever voltage drives that same current through the 500 k$\Omega$ resistor, including its sign.

The 500 k$\Omega$ resistor is the feedback resistor: it returns a fraction of the output voltage to the inverting input, making the amplifier a negative-feedback inverting amplifier. It sets the closed-loop gain, here $-R_f/R_{in} = -500/25 = -20$, and stabilises that gain against changes in the op-amp's open-loop gain while keeping the circuit in its linear range. (b)

The output is fed back to the $-$ input, so any change in output is opposed, which stabilises the gain and keeps the amplifier linear. The magnitude of the gain is set by the ratio of the two resistors, not by the op-amp itself.

content.text: Determine the output voltage, $V_{out}$.
