content.text: A student constructed the following circuit in which four different logic gates were used. The circuit had two inputs, A and B, and one output, S. For each of the possible input states of A and B, construct a truth table showing the output of Gate 1 at P, Gate 2 at Q, Gate 3 at R and Gate 4 at S.

content.alt_text: Logic circuit with inputs A and B. Gate 1, a NAND, takes A and B and gives output P. Gate 2, a NOT, takes A and gives Q. Gate 3, a NOR, takes B and Q and gives R. Gate 4, an OR, takes P and R and gives the final output S. A key table lists Gate 1 NAND, Gate 2 NOT, Gate 3 NOR, Gate 4 OR.

content.text: Build the table one column at a time, starting with the gate nearest the inputs, and evaluate every gate for all four input combinations before moving to the next column.
Use the key: NAND is 0 only when both inputs are 1; NOT simply flips; NOR is 0 whenever both of its inputs are 1.
When the table is complete, check whether any row gives $S = 0$ and say what that tells you about the circuit as a whole.

Gate 1 is a NAND of A and B, so P = 1 except when A = B = 1. Gate 2 is a NOT of A, so Q = 1 when A = 0. Gate 3 is a NOR of B and Q, so R = 0 only when B = 1 and Q = 1, that is when A = 0 and B = 1. Gate 4 is an OR of P and R, and since P and R are never both 0 the output S is 1 for every input combination. The circuit therefore acts as a 1-detector.

content.text: Discuss the possibility that there may be a limit on the growth of computer power.
Do not treat computer power as clock speed alone - memory, storage, the transfer of data between chips, and the number of components are all part of it.
For each limitation, state the physical reason as well as the limitation: what happens to the heat produced, and what happens to a transistor as its dimensions shrink?
The top band also asks what could replace the present technology, so name at least one alternative and say what it does differently.

Speed is limited by the distance a signal can travel in the time available, so raising the clock frequency raises the power dissipated in a chip; the resulting heat must be removed, and when the heat can no longer be removed the chips melt, which caps the clock rate. Shrinking transistors also approaches the scale at which quantum tunnelling between the source and drain occurs, so leakage current rises and the transistor can no longer switch reliably, so Moore's law cannot continue indefinitely. The number of transistors that can be connected is limited by the heat released from a chip and by the difficulty of interconnecting very large numbers of them, so data transfer between chips limits performance. Increasing the clock frequency is already less effective than adding cores, because of the limits of parallel programming, and memory and bandwidth become the bottleneck for many tasks. Possible alternatives include parallel and distributed computing, optical interconnections, quantum computing using superposition and entanglement, DNA or biological computing, and specialised processors such as graphics processing units, which trade generality for efficiency.

A strong answer explains the physical reasons for each limitation and mentions at least one alternative technology. Examiners reported that this part was answered quite poorly, with vague generalisations and discussion confined to speed increases without looking at other elements of computer power such as memory, storage and interconnection.

3-4 marks: demonstrates a basic knowledge of limitations to the growth of computer power and the reasons, and may mention alternative technologies.
1-2 marks: mentions only a few limitations, OR discusses computing power in terms of either speed or memory only.

content.text: Discuss the impact that developments in electronics have had on society.
Separate the question into two halves: first the key developments in electronics themselves - components, circuits and systems - and only then their impact on society.
Balance the impact. For each advance ask who gained, who lost, and what new problems it created.
A list of household appliances is not an answer: the question asks about developments in electronics and the difference those developments made.

Key developments include the transistor, which made small, cheap and reliable electronics possible; integrated circuits and the microprocessor, which put a computer on a single chip; the development of fibre optics, satellites and digital mobile telephony, which together gave instant global communication; digital computing, the internet and e-commerce; and the development of sensors, actuators, solid-state devices and large-scale automation. The impact on society has been profound. Global communication has collapsed distance: people can be in instant contact across the world for voice, text and video, and knowledge and culture are shared globally. Money, banking, records, commerce and employment have been transformed, and education, medicine, transport, entertainment and agriculture have all been made faster, safer and more accessible, as in automated control of manufacturing, medical monitoring and navigation. On the other hand electronics has produced new social problems: it has displaced workers whose jobs have been automated, it has concentrated wealth in the companies that own the networks and data, and it has created surveillance through cameras and tracking, cyber-crime and the theft of personal data. It has been used for warfare through drones and cyber-attacks, and it has contributed to misinformation and the erosion of public trust through social media. The very concentration of manufacturing in the electronics industry has left supply chains vulnerable. The industry also consumes non-renewable materials and creates e-waste, and constant upgrading and disposal of devices adds to environmental pressure. Hence the impact is a double-edged one whose balance depends on how societies choose to regulate and use these developments.

A strong answer describes a number of key developments, not merely a list of appliances that use electronics, and then discusses their social impacts, balancing benefits and problems. Examiners reported that many candidates confused 'developments in electronics' with 'use of electronics' and with electricity, so weaker responses were simply a list of household appliances or electronic equipment.

items: 7-8 marks: demonstrates an extensive knowledge, describes a number of key developments in electronics, and discusses their social impacts in a coherent way.
5-6 marks: demonstrates a thorough knowledge, describes some of the key developments in electronics, and discusses their social impacts.
3-4 marks: demonstrates a sound understanding of the way in which electronics has affected society, but mentions only a few examples of developments in electronics or the discussion is not coherent.
1-2 marks: provides only a couple of examples of developments in electronics, or gives a cursory discussion of their social impact, or does not make clear the impacts on society.
